fields.explanation:
The proof's step has the form 'P ⟹ 51 ≤ 50', used as a reductio: since 51 ≤ 50 is false, P is meant to be false. That inference is only usable if the implication is sound, which here would require P itself to be false. P is TRUE by exact integer arithmetic, so 'P ⟹ false' is itself a false implication and the line establishes nothing.

The underlying identity is the binomial absorption identity n·C(n−1,k−1) = k·C(n,k). With n = 100, k = 50 it gives 100·C(99,49) = 50·C(100,50), so the displayed inequality C(100,50)·1 ≤ 100·C(99,49) is exactly C(100,50) ≤ 50·C(100,50), i.e. 1 ≤ 50 after cancelling the positive factor C(100,50). It holds with a large margin (the gap is 4943675882732645473405812365544). Since the double-counting inequality is satisfied, whatever configuration it was meant to rule out is not ruled out by this line, and the argument has a gap at this step.

fields.flaw: The proof claims the double-counting inequality C(100,50)*1 <= 100*C(99,49) implies 51 <= 50, i.e., that it is contradictory. In fact 100*C(99,49) = 50*C(100,50), so the inequality is true (it reduces to 1 <= 50) and yields no contradiction.
fields.problem: We are labelling some subsets from set $\{1,2...,100\}$. Prove that...
fields.source_context:
0001 | >Let $S = \{1, 2, 3, ..., 100\}$ and $P$ is the collection of all subset $T$ of $S$ that have $49$ elements, or in other words: $$P = \{T \subset S : |T| = 49\}.$$ Every element of $P$ is labelled by the element of $S$ randomly (the labels may be the same). Show that there exist subset $M$ of $S$ that has $50$ members such that for every $x \in M$, the label of $M -\{x\}$ is not equal to $x$

We make a bipartite graph, one side with subsets $M$ of $S$ with power $50$ and the other is set $S$ it self. We connect $M$ with $s\in S$ iff labelling $M -\{s\}$ is $s$.

0011 | By assumption, every $M$ has degree at least $1$, and every element $s$ in $S$ has degree at most ${99\choose 49}$, so we have $${100\choose 50}\cdot 1\leq 100\cdot {99\choose 49}\implies 51\leq 50,$$

fields.witness:
The witness is the exact-integer evaluation of the proof's own displayed inequality at its own instance (n,k) = (100,50). The proof asserts 'C(100,50)·1 ≤ 100·C(99,49) ⟹ 51 ≤ 50', i.e. treats the inequality as contradictory. Exact computation gives

  LHS = C(100,50)·1  = 100891344545564193334812497256
  RHS = 100·C(99,49) = 5044567227278209666740624862800
  RHS − LHS          = 4943675882732645473405812365544 > 0
  RHS/LHS            = 50 exactly

So the antecedent LHS ≤ RHS is TRUE while the consequent 51 ≤ 50 is FALSE; the displayed implication is therefore false. Equivalently the absorption identity holds at this instance: 100·C(99,49) = 50·C(100,50), so dividing the displayed inequality by the positive integer C(100,50) yields exactly 1 ≤ 50, not 51 ≤ 50. The selected Lean theorem is ¬printedImplication, where printedImplication is (choose 100 50 ≤ 100 · choose 99 49 → 51 ≤ 50); its proof establishes the antecedent by exact arithmetic.
